blocks.1: In older times people were careful to keep up the customs they inherited from their parents, but over time many of the old customs have nevertheless disappeared. As early as 1900 “Fremad” called for the old village customs to be preserved, but unfortunately that has been done only to a small extent.
blocks.3: From the earliest times the village was divided into “bearlag”, invitation circles, that is, areas that belonged together when inviting people to funerals, weddings and other gatherings. On such occasions they apparently invited many from the various holdings.
blocks.4: It has been hard to find out about these circles now. Hilda Brosvik says that at a death at Henriksbø they invited 2 people from each house at Henriksbø and Undertun and 1 from each house at Indre Midtun. She says that, as far as she can remember, it was a little different at weddings; then these boundaries were not always followed so strictly.
blocks.5: No one can now say for certain how it was on the other farms in Midtunvågen, but from the conversations I have had with some of the people who live here, it seems that, at least at funerals, it may have been like this:
blocks.6: Henriksbø invited 2 from each house at Henriksbø and Undertun and 1 from each house at Indre Midtun.
blocks.7: Indre Midtun invited 2 from each house at Midtun and Gryta and 1 from each house at Øvre Henriksbø.
blocks.8: Ytre Midtun 2 from each house at Midtun and Gryta and 1 from each house at Nedre Henriksbø.
blocks.9: Gryta 2 from each house at Gryta and Midtun, 1 from each house at Undertun.
blocks.10: Undertun 2 from each house at Undertun and Henriksbø and 1 from each house at Gryta.
blocks.11: Flolid shared an invitation circle with Svaberg, Glosvik, Nyborg and Fonna.
blocks.12: Svaberg invited from Flolid and Nese.
blocks.13: Those who lived beyond “Rauleet” formed a circle of their own.
blocks.15: Hilda Brosvik has written about the funeral customs in the 1920s and 30s:
blocks.16: “When there was a death in the neighbourhood, the message went from man to man. A coffin was seldom kept in stock. Sometimes one was got from Skjerjehamn, but usually from Bergen. When the coffin was in place, word was sent to the nearest neighbours that the body would now be laid in the coffin, and that they should come to a gathering. (A viewing, or a service around the coffin, as it is now called.)
blocks.17: Here it was upper and lower Henriksbø that gathered, 2 from each house. People gathered for a short service around the open coffin, where the dead person lay nicely dressed. When the service was over, they said farewell to the dead and put the lid on the coffin. The coffin was then carried into another room. It was the cellar, or an outbuilding, which had been cleared and finely arranged. When that was done, the group gathered for a meal of coffee and food before setting off home.
blocks.18: The funeral day was usually 8 days after the day of death, if nothing stood in the way. Someone from the bereaved household went round inviting those who were to take part. Here at Henriksbø we invited 2 from each house at Henriksbø and Undertun, 1 from each house at Indre Midtun; the parish clerk and the priest were always there. Many relatives were invited. The family was usually large, and invitations went far out along the line. The funeral party gathered at 11 a.m. Then they were to have breakfast. When that was done, the room was cleared for a gathering around the coffin. The priest was there and held a short service; sometimes relatives and family members spoke. After that they were to get ready for the journey to church. They used the horse in those days.
blocks.19: When everything was ready for the drive, the parish clerk and a good singer walked in front of the horse with the coffin. They drove slowly out of the farmyard, the procession was gathered, and as they moved off they sang a hymn verse in farewell; then they went on along the road to church.
blocks.20: When they came to where the village opened out, with a view over to Undertun and in towards Flolid, the procession stopped, sang a hymn, and as it were greeted and took leave there too.
blocks.21: Then they went on to the church, for the usual ritual. When they took the coffin off the wagon at the foot of the path to the church, and on the way up to the church, the funeral party sang as they walked up.
blocks.22: When they were finished in the church and at the grave, the party was to gather again for dinner and coffee in the home. Funerals used to be held around in the homes.
blocks.23: Relatives who had a long way to come had to arrive the evening before the funeral and often had to stay until the day after. Such a funeral meant a lot of bustle and work, with much forethought on the part of the hosts. Everyone wanted to do their best. Neighbours helped each other both with lodging and work.”
blocks.24: She adds: on the farmyard by the house where the dead person belonged, greenery (finely chopped juniper) was strewn for the funeral. In older times the funeral guests from the neighbourhood brought milk or cream with them.
blocks.25: Flowers and wreaths on the coffin were usual, but not in such quantities as today. The wreaths were home-made then. It was not unusual either for flowers to be laid on the coffin with a few words of greeting, both at home before the journey to church and in the church.
blocks.26: When she was a child the flag hung at half-mast all day on the day of the funeral. She cannot remember when it became the custom to hoist the flag to the top after the burial. She seems to remember that at Midtun the funeral procession stopped at Liktua. That would correspond, if so, to what they did at Henriksbø when they looked over to Undertun, to take leave of the rest of the village.
blocks.28: I have got information about this through conversations with people in the village. Here I would especially mention Olav H. Tveit (at Stølen).
blocks.29: A wedding was usually planned well in advance. “They are getting married in the spring”, “in the summer”, “in the autumn” were familiar sayings. Weddings were usually held in the home of one of the couple, and there was a great deal of work in preparing: animals were to be slaughtered, beer brewed and baking done. There were also many other things to arrange. If there was maintenance work that would soon have to be done anyway, such as laying a new floor, new cladding, painting or the like, this was often done for the wedding too. Some had to go to the forest for timber and to the sawmill to get materials. If they had no flagpole, that too was often seen to for a wedding. “The flagpole came the year Per got married”, people remembered.
blocks.30: The engaged couple also “got themselves ready”, as people said, that is, they prepared for marriage, for setting up their own home. A great many things were needed, both sewn, knitted and woven articles and other household goods. Usually they made much of the furniture at home. The invitations to the wedding were made by the couple, or one of the parents, going from house to house and inviting the guests “in person”. Guests who lived outside the village were invited by ordinary letter. It was important that no one was forgotten, either among family or neighbours. The invitation of neighbours largely followed the invitation circles, but at weddings others were often invited as well, for example people one saw a lot of. The customs of the circles determined how many were to be invited from each house. If it did not suit the people of the house themselves to come, others came, for example grown-up children. Weddings were mostly for adults; of children, usually only those belonging to the wedding farm and the closest family attended.
blocks.31: It was usual for guests from outside to come the day before the wedding party. All lodging was in private homes; those who could not be fitted in at the wedding farm got rooms with the neighbours, and every usable sleeping place was put to use.
blocks.32: The wedding day began with breakfast for all the visiting guests. The bride was dressed by women who were experienced in such things. The most usual from of old were crowned brides, but gradually it became just as common to have a “white bride”, as they said, that is, the bride wore a veil. Especially in the time after the war of 1940–45 the veil took over more and more, but some kept to the tradition of the crown. Since it became rather heavy for the bride to wear the crown all day, she often took it off as the day wore on.
blocks.33: As the guests gathered they were given something to “bite” and to drink, but they were careful with the beer before the ceremony. The bridal procession walked to church with fiddlers at its head and the bridal couple at the front. The custom of parents accompanying, “leading”, bride and groom to the altar was not usual here, but it happened. The bridal couple walked arm in arm across the church floor to a wedding march from the church organ. Usually the wedding ceremony took place at 2–3 o'clock on a Saturday afternoon, sometimes earlier in the day. After the ceremony the procession went back to the wedding farm, where the cooks and their helpers waited with dinner. On the way home from church 3 shots were fired. At home it was now the master of ceremonies who received and welcomed the guests to the wedding party. His task was to make people feel at home and enjoy themselves. Sometimes the bridal couple and guests were received with cheers.
blocks.34: It was important that the master of ceremonies was a good singer so that he could get the songs going easily and smoothly. In earlier times printed wedding songs were not usual. They used ordinary songs that people knew, both at the dinner and the coffee table. The main course at dinner was a meat dish, often meat in gravy, and then there was dessert, often a fruit compote. The dinner lasted about a couple of hours. The time often varied somewhat from wedding to wedding, depending on how many made speeches. The master of ceremonies kept people “going” with jokes of various kinds, and he would often get the guests up to make speeches, but this varied from party to party depending on how the company was made up. Some found it easy to speak, others did not. It was usual for the fathers of the bride and groom to speak at dinner, and perhaps one of the siblings of each of the couple, while others might wait until the coffee table, when the mood had usually become a little “looser”.
blocks.35: Between dinner and coffee the time passed in “talk and good company”; people liked to stretch their legs and walk about a little. If the weather was fine they often stayed outdoors, strolling about, chatting and joking. The bridal couple went round offering a dram and wine to the guests, and in the cellar the barman was busy pouring beer. Drinks were served both with and without alcohol. In the bridal room one got a bridal dram and wine (with and without alcohol). The gifts were displayed there. The gifts could be, then as now, money or things. Gift vouchers did not come into use here until many years after the last world war. In the years around 1930 money gifts could vary from about 20 kroner up to as much as 30 kroner. Considering people's incomes at that time, 25 kroner, for example, would correspond to about 3 days' pay for an ordinary wage earner.
blocks.36: With the coffee there were home-baked cakes of many kinds, a lot of yeast baking, and lefse of various sorts, as well as sweet bread. In older times there were not so many cream cakes. This may be because, despite good, cool cellars, it was not so easy to store these cakes for any length of time. Weddings were mostly in summer, and there were no fridges or freezers.
blocks.37: During the coffee there could also, as mentioned, be speeches. It was now usually more “uninhibited” speakers who took the floor, and the speeches could be of a “lighter” kind, often amusing, and created a good festive mood. After the coffee the room was cleared for dancing. On the farms they had often made a dance floor in the barn. Weddings were often held between the spring work and haymaking, and then the barn was empty and the animals out grazing. The hay floor of the barn was often used as a dance floor.
blocks.38: Later in the night, around one or two o'clock, came the midnight meal, sour cream porridge with cured meats. Before the porridge, 3 shots were fired again. After the midnight meal the dancing went on until morning.
blocks.39: There was often a good deal of fun during the wedding party. For example it was common for someone to try to “steal” the porridge. Stealing spoons was also a common sport. The cooks had to keep a close watch. The “stolen” goods turned up again afterwards. Other “pranks” might be thought up too. Sometimes people dressed up and made fun that way, often with songs and/or story-telling. It was not unusual either for young people to go “gatecrashing” at weddings. They came uninvited to the wedding late in the night, often in disguise, and made a lot of fun at the party. They were well received with food and drink.
blocks.40: Now and then the various pranks could perhaps be a little on the coarse side, but as a rule everything went fine, without anyone feeling offended, and at any rate it created life, bustle and atmosphere at the party.
blocks.41: For the visiting guests, as mentioned, beds were arranged. Usually “Slunkebol” (makeshift beds on the floor with straw in them) were also made up, for example in the loft, and there the young people usually slept. Some played tricks on those who had gone to bed, hiding shoes or clothes, for example. Many did not go to bed at all; they stayed up until the next day, when the visiting guests gathered at the wedding farm for a meal. Guests from the village who wished to came too, and there was usually a dance this day as well. There was plenty of food and drink. It did not always suit the visitors to get away, so they often stayed on until the following day, depending on how their travel arrangements worked out.
blocks.42: After the community hall came, it became common for the hosts to hire rooms there for the wedding party.
blocks.43: Not all weddings were equally big, but it was not unusual to have up to, and even over, 100 guests. The wedding of the eldest of the children, or of the one who would live on the farm, tended to be the “grandest”.
blocks.44: Celebrating a wedding could be both tiring and expensive, but it was a fine occasion for family, neighbours and friends to gather. New acquaintances were made, which perhaps in turn led to new wedding parties. Many good memories were surely tied to these pleasant festive gatherings.
blocks.45: In the journal of the historical society for Sogn, no. 19, 1958, Odd Nordland writes interestingly about a wedding in “Dahl's Evindvig”. The starting point for the article is a song from the wedding. The bride wore a crown, the bridal couple rode to and from church, and on the way home the horse was frightened by the salute so that the bride fell off. It does not say on which farm the wedding was held, but the farm must have lain so that it was natural for the couple to ride to church.
blocks.46: The author of the song was a guest at the wedding, but his name is not known. He was probably a friend or relative of the parish clerk and his wife here, Furnæs, who lived in Fonnevika. Nor is it known when the wedding took place; it was probably in the 1840s.
blocks.47: The song and the article are very interesting, but it would be far too much to quote here.
blocks.49: Births took place at home. Then they had to fetch the midwife, often in a great hurry; in my childhood she lived at Dalsøyra. There was great excitement and expectation around births, of course first and foremost for the mother herself, but everyone else on the farm was also affected by what was about to happen.
blocks.50: It was important that everything was well prepared, with nappies, towels, baby clothes etc. The mother-to-be, the housewife, had seen to such things herself. She had also made sure there was plenty of easy food in the pantry. During the birth itself the house had to be well heated, and a good supply of hot water was important.
blocks.51: There was surely many a nervous waiting father who paced about, fed the stoves with wood, wrung his hands, listened at the door of the room where the birth was taking place, and could at last breathe out when a smiling midwife opened the door and said that everything was now safely over. An exhausted but happy mother lay smiling with a newborn baby in her arms, and the tiny cries of the baby spread joy through the house; a cheerful, light mood came over everyone.
blocks.52: There is a story from a birth – I do not think it is true – but it goes like this:
blocks.53: It had been a rather hard birth. Right after the baby had come into the world the midwife gave it a little smack on the bottom (they often did this to get the breathing started). A boy who saw this said: “Oh, give him another one – what on earth was he doing in there?”
blocks.54: If anything, this story must be of more recent date; in older times it was usual for only the midwife and the helpers to be present at births.
blocks.55: In the time after the birth the neighbouring women came on a “lying-in visit”. They brought “bed food”, usually sour cream porridge (with lots of fat on it), which they carried in wooden containers or bowls. Bringing food was an old custom rooted in the importance of the mother getting enough good nourishment to provide plenty of milk for the baby and to get quickly “back on her feet” after pregnancy and birth.
blocks.56: Later it became more common to bring gifts for the baby, mostly clothes of various kinds.
blocks.57: Three or four months after the birth it was usual to carry the child to baptism. A christening was a great occasion. Families often had a christening gown and bonnet that were handed down; it became a family tradition to use them. These gowns and bonnets were finely made, often with lace and finery, and they were, as far as I can remember, almost always white. There were usually 5 godparents: a godmother (the one who carried the child to baptism), a woman who helped take the christening bonnet off and on, and 3 men. These 5 took on the responsibility for the baptism that the priest reminded them of during the ceremony. Baptism was almost always performed during a service, but christenings were sometimes held on weekdays too. If it was urgent to give the child a name, for example if the child was weak and there might be doubt whether it would survive, a home baptism was sometimes performed.
blocks.58: After the service at which the christening took place, the christening guests gathered at home for a pleasant time with dinner and coffee. The guests were mostly the godparents and the closest family. The baptised child received gifts on the day of the christening; they might be things they would later need in daily life, and girls also often got ornaments. In older times it was usual for people to brew beer for christenings, as for other family occasions, and indeed for funerals too. We know the words “barsøl” (christening ale) and “gravøl” (funeral ale), which show that beer was used on such occasions. I cannot remember beer being served at funerals; that custom had surely long since gone, but at christenings there was often beer for those who wanted it, usually “bought beer”. In our parts the bought beer came from Hansa Brewery in Bergen.
blocks.59: An old custom was the “churching” of women in the church after childbirth and baptism. Anna Nyhammer remembered this custom: at the service where the churching took place, the priest spoke to the women who had given birth and carried children to baptism, and led them, one by one, into the church while a hymn was sung. The hymn used was called something about “Mothers' churchgoing”.
blocks.61: Confirmation in Gulen church. Photo: Unknown.
blocks.62: After finishing primary school, the children were confirmed at the age of 14. Those who had not turned 14 by the day of confirmation had to apply to the king for permission to be confirmed, or else wait another year. Confirmation was usually at the end of August or in September. All through the summer the confirmands from the whole parish gathered in the church for instruction; in my day this was every Monday. In everyday speech this was called “going to the parsonage” or “going for the priest”. In addition to book learning, we also got to know each other during this time.
blocks.63: Confirmation Sunday could be a hard day; both the public examination and the confirmation ceremony took place on this day. During the examination the confirmands stood in two rows along the aisle of the church, and the priest walked between the rows and asked his questions on the material we had learned over the summer. He often walked up and down twice, so it could be hard to stand so long, especially if it was hot.
blocks.64: In earlier days those who could not answer were not “allowed through by the priest”. Everyone was to have a minimum of biblical knowledge, and sometimes they had to come back for several years before they were confirmed. But this must be a long time ago.
blocks.65: In older times the confirmands were also placed on the church floor according to their knowledge; the best stood at the front. Then it happened, from what is said, that some farmers would give the priest a fat billy goat, a calf or something else so that their son would get first place on the church floor on confirmation Sunday. I have heard of people who felt unfairly treated and wrongly placed for such reasons.
blocks.66: After the confirmation service it gradually became usual for the confirmands to be photographed with the priest on the church steps before people went home to the parties in the confirmands' homes. These parties may have varied a little, but here a good meat dinner was usual, and later coffee with cakes of “every kind”.
blocks.67: It was usual for the confirmands to exchange greetings with what were called “confirmation cards”. These cards were folded, had pictures, usually with a biblical motif, and inside a hymn verse was printed. At least one side had space for personal greetings. Sometimes the greetings were written in rhyme, as greetings for weddings often were too. It was also usual for family and friends to give the confirmands such cards or send greetings in the form of greetings telegrams. The guests and the closest family gave the confirmands gifts; they might be useful things, ornaments or money. Later gift vouchers were much used at confirmations, as on many other occasions.
blocks.68: It was usual for boys to get a new suit, often their first, for confirmation; the girls had fine dresses. The custom of confirmation gowns did not come here until 1962. For a time it was not unusual for boys to get a watch for confirmation, often called a “confirmation watch”. Those were pocket watches in those days. The trousers had a special little pocket in the waistband for the watch, and the watch chain usually hung in a small loop down from the belt. If one wore a waistcoat, one of the waistcoat pockets was usually used as a watch pocket, and then the watch chain usually hung in a large loop across the waistcoat, from one pocket to the other.
blocks.69: As part of the confirmation ceremony the confirmands and their closest family, usually the parents, and anyone else who wished, also gathered in the church on the Monday after confirmation Sunday. Then the confirmands, and anyone else who wished, went to the altar and received communion. This day too there was good food and some celebration in the confirmands' homes. Many visiting guests often stayed on for this day too.
blocks.71: A custom that most people still remember, but which has now died out, was the smudge fire when the cows were left out, as mentioned before. It was usual in my childhood too. It really looked as if the herds understood that when the smoke from the fire spread, it was a sign that they were now to stay out for the rest of the summer.
blocks.72: There was always one cow in each herd that wore a bell. It was usually the calmest and “wisest” cow that got the bell round her neck, and I actually think the cows felt it an honour to wear the bell. The one chosen as bell cow usually kept that “office” as long as she was in the herd. It seemed quite clear that if the bell was moved to another cow, the one who lost the bell felt it as a disgrace.
blocks.73: The custom of lighting a bonfire on midsummer eve was held every year, and still is. In old times they lit the midsummer bonfire on Lifjellet above Midtun, but as I remember, Vardehaugen in Neset was the regular bonfire site for many years. For midsummer “rømmask” (sour milk curds) was set, and after the bonfire on Vardehaugen people went to the community hall for "rømmask" with sugar on it and flatbread, and afterwards a little dance. There was a lot of work in gathering material for the midsummer bonfire, a job the children took an active part in. All sorts of things were collected, mostly old junk that people wanted to get rid of, and we carried or pulled it into place on handcarts. Sometimes the young people used horse and cart too, especially if there were bigger things, such as old rowing boats, to go on the fire. We were lucky if we got such an old boat, well soaked in tar; it made the fire last a long time. Bonfires were sometimes also lit on the eve of St Olav's Day, but that was rarer, and then mostly smaller fires.
blocks.74: At Christmas it was usual to hang out sheaves of grain for the small birds. One of the finest birds in these sheaves, I thought, was the yellowhammer. There were a lot of yellowhammers when I was growing up. Now it is very rarely seen here. Another small bird I miss is the corncrake. Its “creaking” song along the field edges on summer evenings is no longer heard. A bird that was not here 50 years ago is the lapwing. There are a lot of them now.
blocks.75: On Christmas Eve the animals usually got an extra treat and a few extra strokes of the brush. Christmas was the greatest festival of the year. There was a tremendous effort with cleaning, cooking and all sorts of preparations well in advance. The children thought the wait was long; they counted the days to Christmas Eve and looked forward excitedly to the festival and the Christmas presents. Between Christmas and New Year many dressed up and went “julebukk” (Christmas mumming). One explanation of this custom I have heard is that it is a remnant from ancient times, when the poor, at this holy time of year, were allowed to go begging from house to house to get a little extra food.
blocks.76: Christmas Eve was full of festive spirit, with a decorated tree and “light in every corner”. Before electricity came we had small live candles on the Christmas tree, standing in candleholders with clips fastened to the branches of the tree.
blocks.77: Before the church bells rang in the holy day (at 5–6 p.m.), those who had any of their own buried there went to the churchyard and decorated the graves. It was not usual to have a service on Christmas Eve then, but Christmas Day was the great holy day when “everyone” went to church.
blocks.78: How people celebrated Christmas Eve could vary from house to house. The usual thing was for families to gather at home, each on their own. Grandparents, and close relatives who had no family of their own, belonged too. At midday there was usually a simple meal, often porridge. Christmas dinner was usually after the animals had been seen to in the evening. Many began the festival by reading the Christmas gospel. Later there was coffee with all kinds of good cakes. In most houses there was a lavish array of Christmas baking and lots of other “treats”, such as nuts and fruit of various kinds. The high point for the children was surely the opening of presents. Some had a visit from Father Christmas on that occasion.
blocks.79: Almost everyone also gathered to walk round the Christmas tree, and there was a lot of singing. People providing the singing and music themselves on various occasions has probably declined as radio, and later television and video, became common in the homes. At Christmas many books and other reading matter came out. The Christmas annuals, for both adults and children, were widely read. In the time after Christmas it used to be common to invite each other to Christmas parties.
blocks.80: For a time there was a regular Christmas party at the youth society on the evening of Boxing Day. At this party the priest usually held a short service, the youth society's paper came out, there were usually readings and various other items, most often plays, and then there was walking round the Christmas tree and much singing and music. After an organ came to the community hall, the teacher played for the singing. Coffee and food were of course a fixed feature.
blocks.81: In “Fremad” I have read that it was an old custom to shoot the old year out. This was done after dusk had fallen on New Year's Eve, but before the church bells rang in the holy day.
blocks.82: In older times too a midnight service on New Year's Eve was usual. New Year's Eve was also a festive day in the homes. There were fireworks, but not in such quantities as today. The children made snow lanterns, small towers of snowballs, in which they put candles. They shone beautifully in the gardens, not only on New Year's Eve but also at other times when we took pleasure in making them. After the hotel (the inn) came, many celebrated New Year's Eve there.
blocks.83: On New Year's Day there was a service. In the afternoon the children's Christmas party was held. As told earlier, there were many items of various kinds at this party, performed by the children themselves and rehearsed over a long time with the teacher. These parties were very popular, as children's parties are today.
blocks.84: At Christmas time a dance was also usually arranged. The parties at Christmas tended to be a “meeting point” between the villagers and those who had moved away and came home for Christmas.
blocks.85: Another party that was held every year was the Mother's Day party. There Mother was the focus; she went to the party free, and the programme was largely arranged in her honour.
blocks.86: There was usually a dance at Easter, and then of course the 17th of May party. The autumn party was also held every year. During the war (40–45) it was forbidden to celebrate the 17th of May, but in 1942 the day was celebrated in Midtundalen. We walked in procession under the flag and the youth society's banner from the community hall, along the path all the way to Ole-selet. Many people took part, and the path was narrow, so it became quite a long procession. During the procession salutes were fired as usual on the 17th of May. On the way in, a German plane flew over the valley. So that we would not be discovered, the procession stopped until the plane had gone. On the summer-farm field there were various items. The parish priest Vatne gave a short sermon. I believe the old sheriff, Bredvik, also gave a short speech. There was a lot of community singing, singing games on the green in front of the hut door and games of various kinds, long jump and triple jump on the slope by the hut and a cross-country race from Ole-selet, round Jakob-selet and back. Inside the hut sour cream porridge was cooked, which, with juice, was sold for 50 øre a plate. One of those who carried in the sour cream says that 25 litres of sour cream were used. I remember that a raffle was held, and one of the prizes was a free tooth extraction at the district doctor's – there was no dentist here then – and another prize was a free trip to Bergen on M/K “Sognnes”.
blocks.87: Several pictures were taken at the gathering. The picture reproduced in this booklet (in the section on memories of the war) was probably taken by the teacher Hansen. He was the driving force at this event too. Even though not quite all the participants are in the picture, it shows that a lot of people had gathered. I think almost everyone who could turned up on this special and fine day, probably the largest gathering of people there has ever been in Midtundalen.
blocks.88: An alternative celebration of the 17th of May at "Ole-selet" in Midtundalen in 1942. A similar picture with the names of the participants is held at the County Archives, SFFf-1994274.0004. Photo: Kristian Hanssen.
blocks.89: The custom of strewing and ringing bells for sweethearts was at least as common before as now. Once when a suitor was visiting a girl on one of the holdings at Midtun, young people in the village dragged his boat up over the bogs, all the way up to “Ospene”, and “moored” it there. I do not know how the fellow got the boat back into the sea, but he certainly needed help.
blocks.90: A good old custom in the village was that people helped each other with voluntary communal work when needed. If a household was struck by misfortune, illness or death, they got help with the work on the farm (spring work, haymaking, harvest) from teams of volunteers. Voluntary work was also usual when big jobs were to be done, for example house building, major repairs and so on. A fine custom that is still a little alive.
